analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal taxes on investment gains roughly in half and adjusts asset values for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by the Ways and Means chairman and 82 cosponsors, sat in committee for two years and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let every taxpayer deduct half of their long-term investment gains from taxable income, and would raise the 'cost basis' of stocks and business property to account for inflation, shrinking the taxable gain when assets are sold. It would also let homeowners deduct losses when they sell their main home for less than they paid. In practice, the value of the first two provisions depends on how much someone owns in stocks, businesses, and property — which is concentrated among the wealthiest households.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers with large capital gains — primarily households and corporations that own substantial stocks, businesses, and investment property — would see their tax rate on gains cut roughly in half, with indexing further reducing tax on gains that merely reflect inflation. Homeowners who sell a principal residence at a loss would gain a new deduction [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Allows a 50 percent income tax deduction for net capital gains for both corporate and noncorporate taxpayers [S2].
Requires indexing of the basis of corporate stock and tangible business property held more than one year, using the GDP deflator, so that inflation-driven gains are not taxed [S2].
Allows an itemized deduction for losses on the sale or exchange of a principal residence [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers as a whole, through foregone revenue. Capital gains accrue overwhelmingly to the highest-income households and to corporations, so the cost of the tax cut would fall on the general Treasury while the benefit concentrates at the top.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the existing 50 percent exclusion for gain on certain small-business stock, a targeted break for startup investors, replacing it with a blanket deduction that does not distinguish new investment from existing holdings [S3].

Because the deduction applies to all net capital gains and indexing applies to stocks and business property, the largest dollar benefits go to those with the largest taxable portfolios; households whose income comes from wages get little or nothing from the core provisions.

The capital-loss deduction for principal residences would open a new deduction that primarily benefits homeowners in falling housing markets, a cost the bill's sponsors did not offset in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The principal-residence loss deduction is a genuine, if narrow, benefit to ordinary homeowners. The core of the bill — the 50 percent gain deduction and inflation indexing — is a large tax cut whose value scales with wealth in taxable assets, and the bill contains no offsetting revenue. An honest supporter would acknowledge that most of the benefit flows to top shareholders and corporations while the revenue cost is shared by everyone.

outcome.mechanism: The chairman of the tax-writing committee introduced it on the first day of the new Congress, it sat in his own committee without a markup or vote for the entire two years, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Archer introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
It gathered 82 cosponsors — 79 Republicans and 3 Democrats — within weeks [S4].
Archer delivered introductory remarks on January 24, 1995 [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: the bill was never reported out of committee, never debated, and never voted on before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers as a whole are no worse off, since the revenue was never given away — but the bill's intended beneficiaries, investors with large capital gains and corporations, gained nothing either. No one advanced because the bill simply stalled in the committee chaired by its own sponsor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; no one else gained

for.name: Rep. Bill Archer
for.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the first day of the 104th Congress; as the committee's chairman, he also controlled the agenda that never brought it to a markup.

for.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
for.what_they_did: Made a 50 percent capital gains exclusion a centerpiece of the House Republican 'Contract with America' agenda the new majority was pushing in 1995, the political context in which this bill was introduced.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and took no recorded action — no markup, no report, no vote — for the full two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 79 of the 82 cosponsors were Republicans, with 3 Democrats, and there was never a recorded vote.

industries.note: A 50 percent deduction on capital gains plus inflation indexing would sharply cut taxes on stock profits, a benefit concentrated in taxable portfolios held by wealthier households. The cost shows up as reduced federal revenue that other taxpayers ultimately cover.
The bill explicitly extends the 50 percent capital-gain deduction to corporate taxpayers, halving tax on corporate capital gains.

The bill lets homeowners deduct losses when selling a principal residence, and indexing applies to tangible property including real estate held in business. The residence-loss benefit is small and only reaches sellers in declining markets.
